3. Short facts relevant for the disposal of the Rule is that the petitioner is a company incorporated in Bangladesh under the Companies Act, 1913 and is engaged, inter alia, in acting as Steamer Agents and local ship Agents in respect of MT Warrior which arrived at Chittagong on 23-5-1998 with the manifested quantity of 17,000 metric Tons of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) in bulk for delivery of the said cargo to the consignees receivers at Chittagong. Soon after arrival of the ship with the cargo of CDSO at Chittagong on 23-5-1998 an Ullage Survey was carried out by the Surveyor for the Supplier, Surveyor for the Agents, the Surveyor for the P& I Club, the Surveyor for the Consignees on board the vessel and, according to the Survey report issued by the said Surveyor, the quantity of cargo found on board the vessel MT Warrior at the time of Survey was 16,948 metric tons of CDSO as against the manifested quantity of 17,000 metric tons and the shortage of 52 metric tons of CDSO was well within 1% Ocean Allowance as admissible. A copy of the said Report is annexed to the Writ Petition and marked as Annexure A. The entire quantity of CDSO in bulk found on board the vessel MT Warrior was discharged into the shore tanks and after completion of discharge of CDSO from the mother vessel all her tanks were thoroughly checked and inspected by all concerned and were found to be dry and empty and a certificate to this effect was issued. A copy of the said Dry Tank certificate issued by the Master of the vessel is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure B. On completion of discharge of the cargo of CDSO in bulk into the shore tanks the dip reading of the shore tanks was taken and a shortage of 154.885 metric tons of CDSO was allegedly found short in the shore tanks. A copy of the said shore tank report is annexed to the petition and marked as annexure C. The Deputy/Assistant Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Chittagong issued a Letter of Call being No. S2-191/MCD/98/1833 CUS dated 29-6-1998 to the petitioner relating to the excess shortage of 154.885 metric tons of CDSO alleging involvement of a loss of Government Revenue to the extent of Taka 9,52,084 when the petitioner duly submitted their explanations by their letter RBSL/WARRIOR/538/ 247/98. Copies of the said letter of Call and the letter of Explanation are annexed to the petition and marked as Annexures D and E respectively. The adjudication officer, the respondent most illegally, and without considering the Ullage Survey Report and the Dry Tank certificate and without considering the explanations submitted by the petitioner most arbitrarily imposed a penalty for Taka 9,52,084 for the alleged excess shortage of 154.885 metric tons of CDSO. A copy of the said Adjudication order No. 110 dated 16-3-1999 along with the penalty bill is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexures F and F-1. The petitioner has received two letters from the principal Appraiser on behalf of the Deputy/Assistant Commissioner of Customs (MCD) import being letter No. 52-191- MCD/98 /3300-CUS dated 31-10-1999 and letter No. S2-191/MCD/98/3539/CUS dated 15-11-1999 demanding the deposition of the penalty amount to Taka 9,52,084 within 10 days otherwise necessary stops under section 202 of the Customs Act, 1969 will be taken. A Copy of the said demand notice dated 31-10-1999 and dated 16-11-1999 is annexed to the petition and marked as Annexure G and H respectively. The petitioner filed supplementary affidavit stating that the petitioner may at best be liable for shortage of 52 metric tons of CDSO as per Ullage Survey Report. 

 submitted that in the instant case for the purpose of shortage, 1% of the imported quantity carried by the vessel is allowed as Ocean Allowance must be taken into account, and that the admitted position is that as per declared manifest the quantity imported for Bangladesh was 17000 metric tons of CDSO and as per Ullage Survey the quantity found at the port of Chittagong was 16,948 metric tons and thus there was difference of only 52 metric tons, which was much less than 1%, the permissible limit, and this shortage does not attract the aforesaid provisions of the Customs Act. The learned Advocate submitted that the claimed shortage quantity of 154.885 metric tons has been calculated on the basis of the Survey made on dip tank reading at shore, which is not permissible under any provision of law. It has been submitted that the measurement to determine any actual shortage has to be made on the basis of measurement taken on the basis of same type of calculation or method. 

 5. The Ullage Survey is conducted on board the vessel and such survey is universally accepted for which in the aforementioned provisions of the Customs Act it has been categorically mentioned that the quantity of shortage, if any, has to be found in the conveyance but the Customs authority failed to consider this aspect of the law and accordingly, arrived at a wrong decision. 

 6. The learned Advocate in support of his contention referred to an unreported decision of this court in the case of Seacom Shipping Limited Vs. President, Customs Excise & VAT Appellate Tribunal, Internal Resources Division and others in Writ Petition No. 948 of 1998 vide judgment and order dated 27-7-2005, wherein also a shortage claim was made by the Customs authority on the basis of shore tank measurement and the same was declared to be without lawful authority in making the Rule absolute, wherein their Lordships have accepted the submission of the learned Advocate that the Ullage Survey having not been considered by the Customs authority the shortage as claimed and the penalty as imposed were bad in law, inasmuch as for the purpose of determining shortage, the shore tank survey was not contemplated under item No. 24(ii) of the table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act, 1969 and held that: 

 "In the light of provision of clause 25(ii) of the Table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act, 1969 and in the light of definition of the 'conveyance' as quoted above, it can be said that the shortage, if any, has to be found on board the vessel. Therefore, the Ullage Survey Report on board the vessel 'Botany Trojan' shall prevail against the shore tank survey report in case of any difference in respect of shortage of cargo between the Ullage Survey Report on board the vessel and the Shore Tank Survey Report and that in case the shortage, if any, found in the Ullage Survey on board the vessel is covered by the 2% admissible Ocean allowance then the carrier will not be responsible for any shortage of crude oil found in the Shore Tank Survey Report which is not covered by 1% admissible Ocean allowance and in such case no penalty can be imposed on the carrier or his agent. The respondents have not applied their mind to this aspect of the case." 

 9. The admitted facts are that the vessel carried CDSO and as per declared manifest the cargo quantity was 17,000 metric tons, whereas as per Ullage Survey conducted at the port of loading the quantity measured as 16,948 metric tons and that as per dip reading shore tank measurement the quantity delivered was measured as 16.948/115 metric tons. The learned Advocate submitted that Ullage Survey is a method by which the measurement of the liquid cargo carried by a vessel is taken on board the vessel, which is universally accepted. Thus, as per Ullage Survey, the quantity of CDSO carried to the port of Chittagong was found to be 16,948 metric tons and thus there was actually a shortage of only 52 metric tons, which is negligible and less than the permissible limit of 1% allowed as Ocean Allowance. It further appears that the difference between the declared manifest quantity of 17,000 metric tons and the Ullage Survey Report quantity of 16,948 metric tons, found at Chittagong comes to 52 metric tons, which is also within the permissible limit of 1% allowance as Ocean allowance. The difference in the declared manifest quantity and the dip-reading shore tank measurement quantity shows a shortage of 154.885 metric tons. The learned Advocate referring to the provisions of item No. 24(ii) of the Table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act submitted that such shortage on the basis of shore tank reading is not contemplated by section 156 of the Customs Act and that section 156 of the Customs Act contemplates that measurement must be taken on the conveyance, that is, on board the vessel. In order to appreciate the said submission of the learned Advocate the relevant provision of law i.e. item No. 24(ii) of the Table under section 156(1) is reproduced below: " 

 11. Now, considering the difference between quantity carried 17,000 metric tons and delivery 16,948 metric tons as per the Ullage Survey Report which was calculated at 52 metric tons and which is much less than the permissible limit of 1% compared to the quantity of CDSO carried by the vessel for Chittagong. 

 12. It is to be noted that the petitioner filed supplementary affidavit stating that the petitioner may at best be charged for shortage of 52 metric tons of CDSO on the basis of Ullage Survey Report. 

 13. The measurement of the shore tank has no relevance in the instant case. We get support from the unreported decision to which the learned Advocate referred to (Judgment and order 27-7-2005 passed in Writ Petition No. 948 of 1998) wherein their Lordships in making the Rule absolute have held that in item 24(ii) of the Table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act, 1969 the words "quantity found in the conveyance" means the quantity found as per measurement taken on board the ship as per Ullage Survey method. Therefore, the Ullage Survey Report on board the vessel prevails against the Shore Tank Survey Report. The question of shortage as contemplated by item No. 24(ii) of the Table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act, the 1% admissible Ocean Allowance on the quantity carried by the vessel must be taken into consideration, and therefore the vessel cannot be held responsible for any shortage below 1% and such shortage cannot be said to be an offence committed under item No. 24(ii) of the Table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act. 

 14. On perusal of the impugned order it appears that the Customs Authority due to non-application of mind as to the provision of item No. 24(ii) of the Table under section 156(1) of the Customs Act failed to consider that the shortage, if any, has to be calculated on the basis of the measurements taken on board the vessel i.e. Ullage Survey Report, and such a shortage cannot be calculated on the basis of survey conducted at the Shore Tanks as has been held by their Lordships in the Judgment and order dated 27-7-2005 passed in Writ Petition No. 948 of 1998, mentioned earlier. Thus we find merit in the Rule. 

 The impugned order dated 16-3-1999 under Penalty Bill No. 110, imposing penalty Taka 9,52,084 for the alleged shortage of 154,885 metric tons of CDSO is hereby set aside and the Customs Authority is to make fresh order on the basis of Ullage Survey Report.
